catalog_quote: 1.11.1. Nouns, Pronouns, Adjectives and Numerals. In most multisyllabic nouns, pronouns, adjectives and numerals the stress is placed on either the final or the penultimate syllable. Word-final stress position, which is found in words in all contexts, may be regarded as the basic one. It is the usual position in words of these categories that occur in pause before an intonation group boundary and also in the citation form of nominals. The retraction of stress to an earlier syllable is typically found in words in non-pausal position in the middle of an intonation group or at least within the middle of a syntactic or discourse unit. ... The normal position for the stress in annexation forms of nouns is on the penultimate syllable ... 1.11.3. Verbs. new_statements.rule_in_words: Nominals (nouns, pronouns, adjectives, numerals) and adverbials: basic stress is word-final (citation form, pausal position), retracting to the penult in non-pausal position inside an intonation group. Verbs: stress sits on the root vowel before the last radical (which is the final syllable in suffixless forms such as +qatə́l 'he kills', imperative +qtúl 'kill!'), moving to the first suffix syllable only when that vowel is elided (+qatlá 'she kills'); further pronominal/TAM suffixes leave it in place (+qatə́llu 'he kills them'). Khan's own summaries (2008 Introduction; 2018 p.19) call this 'general placement of the stress in word final position', a defining trans-Zab Jewish feature attributed to Kurdish/Turkic contact.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on secondary stress in the accessible snippets; Khan distinguishes nuclear vs non-nuclear (intonation-group) stress and describes stress groups (numeral + noun, negator + verb) in sec. 1.12.
new_statements.exceptions: Retraction of nominal stress to the penultimate outside pause / mid intonation group (e.g. onto the indefinite marker); verbs keep stress on the root syllable when suffixes are added, so suffixed verb forms are not word-final; stress is morphologically contrastive (Jastrow 1997: J. Azerbaijan zdélu 'they feared' vs zdelú 'their fear'). Snippet vowel diacritics in the verb examples are scanned-rendered ('+qatál' in the raw snippet = Khan's +qatə́l).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress as marked in Khan's text transcriptions; word-final is explicitly the citation-form and pre-pausal position for nominals, with discourse-conditioned retraction inside intonation groups. The sibling catalog entry for Jewish Sanandaj (hula1244), built on Khan's near-identically worded 2009 description, was coded MORPHOLOGICAL; either label is defensible here, fixed-final chosen because the describer himself names word-final as the basic/default position.
new_statements.identity_note: Khan 2008 describes specifically the Jewish dialect of the town of Urmi (NW Iran; speakers recorded in Israel) = NENA database dialect 79 'Urmi, Jewish'; Garbell 1965 and Jastrow 1997 ('Jewish Azerbaijan') cover the wider Jewish Persian-Azerbaijan group (Urmi, Salmas, Bashkale; southern Solduz/Naghada, Šino/Oshnaviyeh, Sablagh/Mahabad). All fall under Glottolog lish1246 Lishán Didán / ISO trg (Northern trans-Zab Jewish NENA). Not to be confused with Christian Urmi (Assyrian Neo-Aramaic, penultimate stress) described in Khan 2016.
